entities.label: Idea
entities.summary:
Anti-communism, a pervasive political and ideological opposition to communism, emerged definitively in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, solidifying its global presence following the 1917 Bolshevik Revolution in Russia. Characterized by a spectrum of critiques ranging from economic objections to collectivism and state control to moral condemnations of totalitarianism and human rights abuses, anti-communism became a defining force in 20th-century geopolitics. Its adherents spanned various political persuasions, including conservatives, liberals, socialists, and anarchists, united by the common goal of preventing communist expansion or overthrowing existing communist regimes. Key figures like Winston Churchill, Ronald Reagan, and Pope John Paul II galvanized this opposition, while organizations such as NATO and SEATO formed bulwarks against perceived communist threats.

Throughout the 20th century, anti-communism manifested in diverse forms, from intellectual and cultural movements critiquing Marxist theory to violent military interventions and covert operations. The interwar period saw the rise of anti-communist sentiment in fascist Italy and Nazi Germany, often conflating communism with Jewish Bolshevism. Post-World War II, anti-communism became the ideological cornerstone of the Cold War, shaping the foreign policies of the United States and its Western allies. This era witnessed McCarthyism in the US, the suppression of communist parties in many Western nations, and proxy wars fought across Asia, Africa, and Latin America, notably in Korea (1950-1953) and Vietnam (1955-1975). Economic strategies, such as the Marshall Plan, were also employed to counteract communist appeal by fostering prosperity.
